title: Concentration and Titration
description: Mol/dm³, g/dm³ and titration arithmetic with end-point reading.

method_card.title: Concentration and Titration
method_card.content:
Concentration tells you how many moles (or grams) of solute are packed into every cubic decimetre of solution. There are two versions of the formula — pick the right one based on what the question gives you.

Recall equations:

  • \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) — concentration in mol/dm³ (moles per litre)
  • \(c_{g} = \dfrac{m}{V}\) — concentration in g/dm³ (grams per litre)
  • \(n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\) — convert mass to moles using relative formula mass

The critical unit rule: Volume must be in dm³. If the question gives cm³, divide by 1000 before using any concentration formula.

Titration four-step pattern:

  1. Find moles of the substance you know (concentration × volume in dm³)
  2. Use the balanced equation mole ratio to find moles of the substance you don't know
  3. Use those moles with the other volume to find concentration
  4. Check units — answer in mol/dm³ or g/dm³ depending on the question

Reading the burette: The end point is where the indicator permanently changes colour. Read the bottom of the meniscus. Titre = final reading − initial reading. Use the mean of concordant (within 0.10 cm³) titres — discard the rough titre.
steps: Convert all volumes from cm³ to dm³ (divide by 1000)
Identify whether the question asks for mol/dm³ or g/dm³
Find moles of the known substance: n = c × V
Apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation
Calculate the unknown: c = n ÷ V or rearrange as needed

exam_context.frequency: High — concentration and titration calculations appear in almost every Chemistry paper

worked_examples.question: A solution contains 0.3 mol of sodium chloride in 600 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.
25.0 cm³ of NaOH solution of unknown concentration is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ HCl. The equation is: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.

4.0 g of NaOH (Mr = 40) is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against H₂SO₄. The titre is 12.5 cm³. The equation is: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the H₂SO₄ in mol/dm³.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find moles of NaOH in the flask
Step 2 — Find concentration of NaOH stock
Step 3 — Find moles of NaOH in the 25.0 cm³ sample
Step 4 — Apply mole ratio to find moles of H₂SO₄

bronze.display: Calculate the concentration (mol/dm³) of a solution containing 0.5 mol of solute in 250 cm³ of solution.
bronze.equation_hint: \(c = n \div V\) (convert cm³ to dm³ first)

misconceptions.message: Convert 250 cm³ to 0.25 dm³ first. Then c = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2.0 mol/dm³.
Concentration = moles ÷ volume, not moles × volume.

bronze.display: How many moles are in 200 cm³ of a 0.25 mol/dm³ solution?
What volume (in dm³) of a 0.4 mol/dm³ solution contains 0.06 mol?
3.65 g of HCl is dissolved in water to make 500 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.
Calculate the number of moles in 4.0 g of NaOH. (Mr: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
A solution has a concentration of 0.5 mol/dm³. How many moles are in 100 cm³?

misconceptions.message: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so divide by 1000. 750 ÷ 1000 = 0.75 dm³.

bronze.display: Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³ of a solution made by dissolving 5.85 g of NaCl in 500 cm³ of water. (Ar: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
bronze.equation_hint: First find moles using \(n = m \div M_r\), then \(c = n \div V\)

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of HCl of unknown concentration is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ NaOH. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) → mole ratio → \(c = n \div V\)

misconceptions.message: Use the HCl volume (25.0 cm³ = 0.025 dm³) in the final step, not the NaOH volume.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ Ca(OH)₂ is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of HCl. Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl.
silver.equation_hint: Apply the 1:2 mole ratio for Ca(OH)₂ : HCl

misconceptions.message: The equation shows 2 moles of HCl per mole of Ca(OH)₂ — double the moles before finding concentration.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄ is titrated against NaOH. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. The titre is 25.0 cm³. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH.
silver.equation_hint: H₂SO₄ : NaOH = 1 : 2 — double the moles of H₂SO₄

misconceptions.message: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.20 × 0.025 = 0.005. NaOH needs double: 0.010 mol. c = 0.010 ÷ 0.025 = 0.40 mol/dm³.
Two moles of NaOH react with every one mole of H₂SO₄. Multiply H₂SO₄ moles by 2 to get NaOH moles.

silver.display: A student carries out three titrations with concordant results of 24.80 cm³, 24.85 cm³ and 24.75 cm³. A rough titre of 25.30 cm³ was also recorded. Calculate the mean titre to use.
silver.equation_hint: Mean of the three concordant results (within 0.10 cm³ of each other). Exclude the rough titre.

misconceptions.message: The rough titre (25.30 cm³) is always discarded. Mean = (24.80 + 24.85 + 24.75) ÷ 3 = 24.80 cm³.
Keep two decimal places for burette readings to match the precision of the equipment.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.08 mol/dm³ KOH is neutralised by HNO₃. KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O. The titre is 20.0 cm³. Calculate the concentration of the HNO₃.
silver.equation_hint: 1:1 ratio. \(n = c \times V\) then \(c = n \div V\)

silver.display: Calculate the concentration in g/dm³ of a solution made by dissolving 10.6 g of Na₂CO₃ in 200 cm³ of water. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
silver.equation_hint: \(c_g = m \div V\) (V in dm³). No need to find moles for g/dm³.

gold.display: 5.3 g of Na₂CO₃ is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl. The titre is 25.0 cm³. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of HCl. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Na₂CO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2. Double the Na₂CO₃ moles to get HCl moles.

gold.display: A student dissolves KOH in water and makes up 500 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of this is titrated with 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ HCl. KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O. Calculate the mass of KOH originally dissolved. (Ar: K = 39, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: You titrated 25 cm³ from a 500 cm³ flask. Scale up: total mol = conc × 0.5 dm³.

gold.display: Calculate the mass of HCl needed to make 500 cm³ of a 0.4 mol/dm³ solution. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)

25.0 cm³ of NaOH is titrated with three concordant titres of 18.70, 18.65 and 18.75 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ HCl. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: Calculate the mean of the three concordant results before using it in the calculation.

gold.display: A student makes up a standard solution of citric acid (Mr = 192) by dissolving 4.80 g in water and making up to 250 cm³. She titrates 25.0 cm³ of this against NaOH; the titre is 30.0 cm³. The equation is: H₃C₆H₅O₇ + 3NaOH → Na₃C₆H₅O₇ + 3H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH.

misconceptions.message: The equation shows 3 moles of NaOH per mole of citric acid. Multiply the acid moles by 3.

gold.display: A student makes up a standard solution of citric acid (Mr = 192) by dissolving 4.80 g in water and making up to 250 cm³. She titrates 25.0 cm³ of this against NaOH; the titre is 30.0 cm³. The equation is: H₃C₆H₅O₇ + 3NaOH → Na₃C₆H₅O₇ + 3H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Three moles of NaOH react with one mole of citric acid — multiply acid moles by 3.
